case_title: Wall Advisory Opinion — applicability of the Fourth Geneva Convention
question: Is the Fourth Geneva Convention applicable in the Palestinian territories that lay east of the 1949 Armistice Line and were occupied by Israel during the 1967 conflict?
facts: The 1949 General Armistice Agreement between Israel and Jordan fixed a demarcation line, the Green Line, between Israeli and Jordanian forces. During the armed conflict of 1967, Israel occupied the territories lying between the Green Line and the former eastern boundary of Palestine under the British Mandate, including East Jerusalem. Both Israel and Jordan were parties to the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 at the time of the 1967 conflict. Israel took the position that the Convention was not applicable de jure to those territories because, under Article 2, paragraph 2, it applies only to the occupation of territory of a High Contracting Party, and Jordan had not been recognised as the sovereign of the territories before 1967.
holding: In its Advisory Opinion of 9 July 2004, the International Court of Justice held that the Fourth Geneva Convention is applicable in any occupied territory in the event of an armed conflict arising between two or more High Contracting Parties, and that it is therefore applicable in the Palestinian territories which before the 1967 conflict lay to the east of the Green Line and which, during that conflict, were occupied by Israel, there being no need for any enquiry into the precise prior status of those territories.

arguments.claim: The Fourth Geneva Convention applies de facto to the territories east of the 1949 Armistice Line occupied by Israel in 1967, irrespective of whether Jordan was recognised as the sovereign prior to occupation.
arguments.reasoning: Article 2(2) of the Convention states that it applies to all cases of ‘occupation of the territory of a High Contracting Party’. International legal practice interprets ‘territory of a High Contracting Party’ to include territories that were under the de jure jurisdiction of a High Contracting Party, even if that jurisdiction was not exercised as full sovereignty. Jordan, as a party to the Convention, exercised de jure authority over the West Bank under the 1949 Armistice Agreement, and thus the occupied territories fell within the scope of the Convention. This interpretation has been consistently affirmed in the jurisprudence of the International Court of Justice and the International Committee of the Red Cross, which treat the Convention’s protections as triggered by the fact of occupation by a High Contracting Party, not by the existence of a prior recognized sovereign state.

arguments.claim: Customary international law incorporates the substantive protections of the Fourth Geneva Convention, making them binding on any occupying power regardless of treaty applicability.
arguments.reasoning: Customary IHL has crystallised the core humanitarian protections of the Fourth Geneva Convention, such as the prohibition of forcible transfer of protected persons and the duty to ensure their humane treatment. These rules are considered jus cogens and therefore apply to all states in situations of occupation, even where treaty arguments are raised. Consequently, Israel’s obligations under the Convention are enforceable as customary law in the occupied Palestinian territories.

arguments.claim: The International Court of Justice’s advisory opinion on the legal consequences of the construction of a wall in the occupied Palestinian territory confirms that the Fourth Geneva Convention applies to those territories.
arguments.reasoning: In its 2004 advisory opinion, the ICJ examined the status of the territories and concluded that they are occupied territory subject to the Fourth Geneva Convention. The Court’s reasoning rested on the factual situation of military occupation and the existence of an occupying power, not on the question of prior sovereign title. This authoritative pronouncement reinforces the applicability of the Convention to the territories east of the Green Line.

arguments.claim: Israel’s own ratification of the Fourth Geneva Convention creates an unconditional legal obligation to apply its provisions to any territory it occupies, regardless of the status of the previous sovereign.
arguments.reasoning: Treaty law binds a party to the obligations contained in the treaty in all circumstances covered by the treaty’s scope. By ratifying the Convention, Israel accepted the duty to respect and ensure respect for the Convention’s provisions in any territory it occupies. The treaty’s own text does not provide an exemption for situations where the prior sovereign’s title is disputed; therefore, the Convention’s applicability follows automatically upon the commencement of occupation.
